title: Enhancing supply chain resilience and efficiency of HVAC systems in semiconductor manufacturing facilities using graph-based large multimodal models
wp_reasoning_0.10.4: The proposed G-LMM is a single unified model trained end-to-end, not a workflow of multiple LLM calls with distinct roles. Section 5.1.2 states: 'End-to-end training is a critical aspect of G-LMMs, enabling the entire model-from multimodal data input to task-specific output-to be trained as a single, unified system.' The architecture (Table 5, Section 5.1.1) is a fixed pipeline-modality-specific encoders (GNN for graph, transformer for text, CNN for image) → cross-modality attention → multimodal fusion → task-specific heads-with no runtime LLM orchestration. No prompt-chaining is present (no fixed sequence of separate LLM calls each processing the previous output); no routing (no LLM classifier dispatching inputs to specialized follow-up LLMs); no parallelization of independent LLM calls/agents (the parallel modality encoders are components of one end-to-end trained model, not separate LLM calls-only the text transformer is LLM-like, and a single LLM-ish component cannot constitute parallel LLM calls); no orchestrator-workers (no central LLM breaks the task down at run time and delegates to worker LLMs); no evaluator-optimizer (no separate LLM evaluator feeds critique back to a generator LLM in a loop-the loss function in Section 5.1.2 is a training objective, not an inference-time workflow). Hence 'none'.

title: A-NSGA-II: an agentic-guided evolutionary framework for multi-objective optimization with application to closed-loop EV supply chains
wp_reasoning_0.10.4: The paper describes a dual-agent system (Initialization Agent and Evolutionary Agent) operating sequentially at different stages of the NSGA-II evolutionary search (Sections 3.1–3.3). The Initialization Agent is invoked once at the start to guide initial population generation; the Evolutionary Agent runs continuously during evolution, interpreting population-state summaries and outputting strategy recommendations. Neither agent processes the other's LLM output directly—the Evolutionary Agent processes population statistics generated by deterministic NSGA-II operations, not the Initialization Agent's textual output—so this is not prompt-chaining. The agents run at different times (not parallelization), there is no central LLM orchestrator delegating to workers, no input classification/routing to specialized follow-ups, and no generator–evaluator LLM pair: the solution generator is the deterministic NSGA-II, while the LLM only evaluates/interprets state and recommends strategies. The Evolutionary Agent operates as a single autonomous agent in a feedback loop with deterministic code (NSGA-II), which the schema classifies as 'none'.
as_reasoning_0.10.4: The LLM-driven agents perform semantic integration and interpretation, and the guided evolutionary search generates the alternative solutions (design phase). Evidence: the Initialization Agent 'invokes the LLM to infer and analyze the distributional characteristics of the initial solution set based on the number of objectives, the types of decision variables, the characteristics of the constraints, and the potential conflict relationships' and then 'generates a set of exploration-oriented initialization guidance strategies' (Section 3.2); the Evolutionary Agent 'performs a high-level interpretation of these summaries' of population diversity, convergence trends, Pareto-front distribution and constraint satisfaction, identifying patterns such as premature convergence (Section 3.3). The NSGA-II core, with agent-guided crossover/mutation and initialization, produces the candidate solution population (alternatives). information-acquisition is absent: no run-time retrieval beyond the given instance — 'no online or offline training process was involved. Its capability relied primarily on the pretrained model itself, together with prompt engineering and chain-of-thought reasoning' (Section 3.1), and no RAG/web/database queries are described (pretrained LLM knowledge is not run-time acquisition; the structured population summaries are just encoding of the given instance). decision-selection is not automated: the system's final output is a Pareto front handed to humans — 'the framework provides decision makers with a more representative set of trade-off alternatives' (Section 5.1.4) — and non-dominated sorting/elitist selection are selection inside the search (? Table 13 lists 'optimal solution under different preference' with weights w1-w3, but no text describes an automated final-choice mechanism, so this is treated as post-hoc/decision-maker analysis). action-implementation is absent: the system only returns/reports the Pareto solutions; no selected network design is written into a real plan, model, or production system.

title: A benchmark of large language models for spatially informed proposal generation in local search for the p-median problem
wp_reasoning_0.10.4: The method (LLM-1Swap, §3.1–3.2, Algorithm 1) uses a single LLM as a 'proposer' inside an iterative optimizer–evaluate–update loop: each iteration makes one LLM call (one of o4-mini, GPT-4.1, or Claude-4.5, benchmarked separately in §4.2) that generates up to K one-swap candidate solutions from the current state and spatial summaries; a deterministic cost oracle evaluates them; a deterministic ε-greedy rule selects; the updated state is fed back into the next prompt (with up to R re-prompts on non-improvement). This matches the schema's 'none' case: 'a single autonomous agent, also when deterministic code validates, repairs or scores its output and feeds back in a loop' (0.10.4). It is not evaluator-optimizer because the evaluator is deterministic code, not an LLM ('Feedback from deterministic code (schema/constraint validation, solver, simulator, repair algorithm) to the generating LLM is not this pattern'). Not prompt-chaining: the same proposer call is repeated in a loop rather than a fixed sequence of distinct LLM calls each processing the previous output. Not routing, parallelization, or orchestrator-workers: the three frontier LLMs are alternative single models run independently as benchmark variants, never orchestrated together, and no LLM classifies inputs or delegates to worker LLMs. Evidence: §3.1 'a framework that treats LLM as a proposer in an optimizer-evaluate-update loop'; §5 'LLM's role is to generate a batch of promising swap proposals, and all objective computations, feasibility checks, and acceptance decisions are performed and determined externally.'
as_reasoning_0.10.4: information-analysis: The LLM's core role is generating alternatives — it integrates and interprets structured spatial summaries (coordinates, bounding box, k-means cluster summary, outliers, facility statistics, worst-assigned points, top gain candidates; §3.3) to propose batches of candidate one-swap solutions each iteration. Anchor (§3.1): 'At each iteration, the LLM proposes a set of candidate solutions based on structured summaries of multiple types of spatial information from the latest search state.' decision-selection: The method itself (external oracle + algorithm, not a human) evaluates every candidate's objective and feasibility, applies the ε-greedy acceptance rule, tracks the best-so-far solution, and outputs a single final facility configuration S*. Anchors (§3.1): 'The objective and feasibility of each new candidate solution are evaluated externally by a deterministic oracle'; (§3.2/Algorithm 1): 'the best-so-far solution f(best) is tracked across iterations' and 'Return S*'. Since no human ranks or filters the alternatives, the system autonomously evaluates, ranks, and recommends one final option, so decision-selection counts (per schema, stages count when any component of the method performs them, incl. the solver/algorithm the LLM drives). ? Uncertainty note: the per-iteration ε-greedy move acceptance is selection inside the search (excluded per 0.10.4), but the final returned solution S* is the single recommended planning option, which is why decision-selection is included. NOT information-acquisition: all prompt components (A)-(I) are deterministic pre-processing/serialisation of the supplied TSPLIB instance data (§3.3, §4.1) — no retrieval, web/API search, or queries beyond the given problem instance — which per schema does not count. NOT action-implementation: the method only returns/reports the selected solution (Algorithm 1: 'Return S*'); no tool call updating a layout, code edit to a deployed model, or triggered action is described, and per schema returning the selected solution does not count.

title: CORTEX-V: A cognitive reasoning toolkit for vision-based, cost-efficient layout optimization
wp_reasoning_0.10.4: CORTEX-V is a single VLLM agent operating in an iterative refinement loop (Sections 4.1, 5, Fig. 3). Each iteration consists of one VLLM call that analyzes the current layout and proposes a machine move; the proposal is then checked and repaired by deterministic code — rectangular collision detection, boundary/obstacle constraint validation, and a 'minimum displacement correction algorithm' (Section 4.1) — with MHC evaluated by deterministic routines, and the outcome fed back into the next prompt ('Contextual Memory Feedback logs outcomes of previous placements, feeding this history into future prompts', Section 5). Per schema (0.10.4), a single autonomous agent whose output is validated, repaired, or scored by deterministic code in a loop is 'none' — this is not evaluator-optimizer (no second LLM evaluates) and not prompt-chaining. The tool invocations (propose_move_machine, analyze_high_flow_pairs, request_MHC_calculation; Section 6.2, 'tool invocation mode is set to auto') are calls to deterministic optimization functions, not separate LLM calls or agents, so no orchestrator-workers, parallelization, or routing patterns are present.
as_reasoning_0.10.4: information-analysis: The VLLM integrates and interprets the multimodal problem representation (flow matrix, constraint set, base64-encoded layout image) and generates layout-improvement alternatives — §4.1: 'the VLLM analyzes this image to detect suboptimal machine placements and inefficiencies using spatial reasoning and pattern recognition'; §4.2: 'This multimodal design integrates mathematical, spatial, and visual information into a unified prompt, enabling the model to perform zero-shot initialization reasoning and make informed layout optimization decisions.' decision-selection: The system itself evaluates candidate moves (via MHC-calculation and flow-analysis tool calls), applies the best move each iteration, and terminates at a converged final layout that it outputs as the recommended solution, with no human ranking of alternatives — §4.1: 'decision-making augmented by tool-calling, where the VLLM simulates layout changes and assesses their impact on MHC'; §4.2 UserPrompt: 'TASK: Analyze layout and propose best machine move'; §6.3/Table 4 and Figs. 10/12 present the system's final chosen layouts (MHC 27,381.79 → 18,616.66; water-dispenser facility layout in §6.5). action-implementation: Selected moves are written into the layout model via structured tool calls plus an automatic repair step, not merely reported — §1 contribution (2): 'enable VLLMs to make optimization decisions through structured function calls rather than textual recommendations'; §6.2: 'the propose move machine function was consistently triggered 100% usage'; §4.1: 'the minimum displacement correction algorithm is triggered to restore constraint compliance' (repair displacement applied to the layout). information-acquisition is NOT selected: all inputs (material flow matrix, machines.json constraints, matplotlib-rendered layout image) derive from the given problem instance; per schema, encoding/serialising the given instance (base64 images, prompt construction) and deterministic pre-processing do not count, and the contextual memory (§5) only logs placements from the current optimization run rather than retrieving from external documents, web/APIs, sensors, or archives of past runs. Minor ambiguity (?) noted: §4.1 describes moves as 'simulated', but the iterative loop updates the current layout between iterations (UserPrompt carries 'Current MHC' and iteration number) and the repair algorithm applies corrections, so tool calls do update the layout, satisfying the schema's explicit 'tool call updating the layout' example for action-implementation.

title: Three-dimensional facility layout optimization using large language model-driven A-star and non-dominated sorting genetic Algorithm-II
wp_reasoning_0.10.4: Coded 'none' — both LLM usages consist of a single LLM role (GPT-4o via public API, §3.2.2/§3.2.3) with feedback coming only from deterministic code, which the schema assigns to 'none' ('deterministic code validates, repairs or scores its output and feeds back in a loop'). (1) LLM-Driven A* (§3.2.2, Fig. 3; §4.2): one prompted LLM invocation generates candidate evaluation functions ('instructing it to output 10 distinct weight combinations', §4.2); the candidates are then scored by deterministically running A* and comparing path length and turn counts, with the best 'selected empirically' (§3.2.2, three-stage mechanism in §4.2). No distinct LLM call evaluates or critiques the generation, so this is not evaluator-optimizer (the schema explicitly excludes deterministic solver feedback to the generating LLM), and not parallelization (the 10 candidates come from a single prompted call; the GPT-4o vs Claude 3.5 Sonnet runs in §4.2 are robustness comparisons across experimental variants, not in-method voting/sectioning). (2) LLM-Driven NSGA-II (§3.2.3, Fig. 5): the same LLM is invoked every 5 generations as an 'online meta-controller' that selects a crossover/mutation probability pair from a discrete action set using feedback (fitness trends s, probability history p, layout feasibility l(t)) computed by the deterministic NSGA-II run — a closed loop between one LLM role and deterministic code, hence 'none' rather than evaluator-optimizer. The two components run sequentially in the pipeline (Fig. 1), but the NSGA-II LLM prompt does not process the A* LLM's output (it receives population statistics), so there is no prompt-chaining; no routing or orchestrator-workers delegation occurs anywhere. Uncertainty: if the 10 candidate functions were produced by 10 independent parallel LLM calls aggregated by selection, 'parallelization' could be argued, but the text indicates a single call returning 10 combinations.
as_reasoning_0.10.4: information-analysis: The LLM (GPT-4o) designs candidate total evaluation functions f(n)=g(n)+h(n) for A* from natural-language objectives (§3.2.2: 'leverages an LLM to automatically generate the total evaluation function f(n)') and interprets live evolutionary signals (fitness trends, probability changes, layout feasibility) to steer NSGA-II (§2.2/§3.2.3: 'the LLM acts as an online meta-controller that continuously observes the evolutionary state... and selects the most appropriate probabilities'). The driven solvers generate the planning alternatives themselves: LLM-Driven A* produces logistics-channel paths and LLM-Driven NSGA-II produces the Pareto set of 3D layouts (§3.2, Fig. 1). decision-selection: The framework's final stage applies AHP to evaluate and rank the Pareto-optimal layout alternatives against engineer-elicited preference weights, identifying the preferred final layout (§3.2: 'the preferred solution is identified based on Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP)'; §4.3: 'under preference D1, the best solution is S1... under preference D2... S2 being the best solution'). This is the final planning decision (choice of layout) performed by a component of the method, so it counts; caveat (?): human experts articulate the preference weights ('we integrate AHP as a structured preference articulation mechanism'), but the multi-criteria scoring and ranking of the final alternatives is executed by the system's AHP step — borderline between system recommendation and human choice, leaning toward counting because the system actively evaluates and ranks the alternatives and recommends one final option rather than merely handing over the Pareto front. Excluded: information-acquisition — all LLM inputs (grid map, logistics flows/costs, evolutionary feedback) derive from the given problem instance; no retrieval, web/API search, or queries to external sources at run time. action-implementation — the selected layout is only reported/visualized (Figs. 13–14, Table 9) and is not written into a plan, model, or deployed system. The LLM's choices of evaluation functions and crossover/mutation probability pairs are selection inside the search and are excluded per 0.10.4.

title: A governed framework combining large language models and human oversight for supplier selection
wp_reasoning_0.10.4: Prompt-chaining: the framework executes a fixed sequence of four distinct LLM modules, each processing previous outputs, with deterministic services and human checkpoints acting as gates between steps (Sections 3.1, 3.3-3.6). M_I (intent/scenario formulation) converts the request q into a candidate scenario; M_W (advisory reweighting) then receives 'the request, initial scenario, base group weights, and a neutral summary of the ranking' (Section 3.3 / E3b), i.e., M_I's scenario output, and returns a bounded adjustment proposal to the deterministic weight controller. Not parallelization: no independent parallel LLM calls are aggregated; evidence extraction is only 'batched by supplier and aspect' (Section 3.8). Not orchestrator-workers: the module pipeline is pre-defined in the architecture; no central LLM decomposes the task at run time and delegates to LLM workers. Not evaluator-optimizer: invalid outputs receive 'one constrained repair attempt using the original input and the validation report' (Section 3.8) - feedback from deterministic schema/constraint validation, which the definition explicitly excludes; no LLM evaluates another LLM's output in a loop (C1-C4 reviewers are humans).
